questions.q: What is the correct interpretation of a $95\%$ confidence interval for a population mean $(42.1, 48.7)$?
choices: We are $95\%$ confident that the true population mean falls between $42.1$ and $48.7$
There is a $95\%$ probability that the true mean is between $42.1$ and $48.7$
$95\%$ of all individual values in the population lie between $42.1$ and $48.7$
$95\%$ of sample means will equal the population mean
questions.answer: Confidence level refers to the long-run success rate of the method: in repeated sampling, $95\%$ of intervals generated will capture the fixed true parameter.

questions.q: In a sample of $100$ items, $\hat{p} = 0.60$. With critical value $z^* = 1.96$, what is the margin of error for a $95\%$ confidence interval for $p$?
How can you decrease the width of a confidence interval?
choices: Increase the sample size or decrease the confidence level
Increase the confidence level or increase the sample size
Decrease the sample size or increase the confidence level
Increase the standard deviation of the data
questions.answer: Width is $2 \times \text{critical value} \times \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. Increasing $n$ shrinks the denominator; lowering confidence level (e.g. from $99\%$ to $90\%$) lowers the critical value.

questions.q: What is the statistical definition of a P-value?
choices: The probability of observing a test statistic as extreme or more extreme than the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is false
The probability of making a Type I error
questions.answer: The P-value is calculated under the assumption that $H_0$ is true, measuring how plausible the observed sample outcome is purely by chance.

questions.q: If a test yields a P-value of $0.023$ and the significance level is $\alpha = 0.05$, what is the conclusion?
choices: Reject $H_0$; there is convincing statistical evidence in favor of $H_a$
Fail to reject $H_0$; the evidence is insufficient
Accept $H_0$ as definitively proven
Reject $H_a$; the test is inconclusive
questions.answer: Because $\text{P-value} = 0.023 < \alpha = 0.05$, we reject $H_0$ and conclude that there is statistically significant evidence for $H_a$.

questions.q: Why do statisticians state 'fail to reject $H_0$' instead of 'accept $H_0$'?
choices: Failing to find sufficient evidence against $H_0$ does not prove that $H_0$ is true
Because $H_0$ is always false in practice
To avoid computing the test statistic
Because the P-value is always approximate
questions.answer: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; we never prove the null hypothesis true, we merely conclude the data is consistent with it.

sections.heading: Section 3: Type I Error, Type II Error, and Power

questions.q: What is a Type I error?
choices: Rejecting the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually true
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually false
Calculating an incorrect test statistic
Using the wrong degrees of freedom
questions.answer: A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting a true null hypothesis. The probability of a Type I error equals the significance level $\alpha$.

questions.q: What is a Type II error?
choices: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when the null hypothesis is actually false
Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
Selecting a biased sample
Misinterpreting the P-value
questions.answer: A Type II error (probability $\beta$) is a false negative: failing to detect a real effect when the alternative hypothesis is true.

questions.q: What is the power of a statistical test?
choices: The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis ($1 - \beta$)
The probability of making a Type I error ($\alpha$)
The sample size $n$
The probability of retaining a true null hypothesis
questions.answer: Power $= 1 - \beta$ represents the test's ability to successfully detect a true difference or effect of a specified magnitude.

questions.q: When estimating a population mean $\mu$ with unknown $\sigma$, which distribution and test statistic are used?
choices: $t$-distribution with $t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}$ and $df = n - 1$
Standard normal distribution with $z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{\sigma / \sqrt{n}}$
Chi-square distribution with $df = n - 1$
$F$-distribution with $df = (n-1, n-2)$
questions.answer: When $\sigma$ is replaced by the sample standard deviation $s$, the standardized statistic follows Student's $t$-distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.

questions.q: How does the $t$-distribution compare to the standard normal ($Z$) distribution?
choices: The $t$-distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped but has heavier tails (more spread)
The $t$-distribution is skewed right
The $t$-distribution has less variability than $Z$
The $t$-distribution is bounded between $-3$ and $3$
questions.answer: The $t$-distribution has heavier tails to account for the extra uncertainty introduced by estimating $\sigma$ with $s$. As $df \to \infty$, $t$ approaches $Z$.

questions.q: A researcher compares scores before and after a training program on the same $20$ subjects. Which test should be performed?
choices: Paired $t$-test on the differences ($d_i = \text{After}_i - \text{Before}_i$)
Two-sample independent $t$-test
Two-sample $z$-test for proportions
Chi-square test of independence
questions.answer: Because the two observations come from the same individuals, the data is dependent (matched pairs), requiring a one-sample paired $t$-test on the pairwise differences.
